title: Exercise 7C · Q3
summary: Convert to a common denominator first, then compare the squares.
alt: Exercise 7C · Q3: In ΔSTU, ST = 7/12 cm, TU = 5/6 cm and SU = 1/3 cm. Is ΔSTU a right-angled triangle?

hyp.label: Hypotenuse
hyp.text: The side opposite the right angle. It is always the longest side.

legA.label: Shorter side 1
legA.text: One of the two sides that meet at the right angle.

legB.label: Shorter side 2
legB.text: The other side that meets at the right angle.

steps.title: The question
steps.narration: **ΔSTU** has **ST = 7/12 cm**, **TU = 5/6 cm** and **SU = 1/3 cm**. Is **ΔSTU** a right-angled triangle?

steps.title: Use a common denominator
steps.narration: Write every side over **12**.\[\begin{aligned}ST &= \tfrac{7}{12} \\ TU &= \tfrac{5}{6} = \tfrac{10}{12} \\ SU &= \tfrac{1}{3} = \tfrac{4}{12}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Find the longest side
steps.narration: The **longest side** is **TU = 10/12 cm**. If ΔSTU is right-angled, TU must be the hypotenuse.

steps.title: Square and add the other two
Compare and conclude
steps.narration: Since **100/144 ≠ 65/144**, **ΔSTU is not** a right-angled triangle.

formulas.title: Pythagoras' theorem
formulas.text: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

formulas.title: Finding the hypotenuse
formulas.text: Add the two squares, then take the square root.

formulas.title: Finding a shorter side
formulas.text: Subtract the known shorter side's square from the hypotenuse's square, then take the square root.

takeaways: Find the **longest side** first — if the triangle is right-angled, that side must be the hypotenuse.
Test it: does the longest side's **square** equal the **sum of the squares** of the other two sides?
If the squares match, the triangle **is** right-angled (opposite the longest side); if not, it isn't.
With **different denominators**, convert every side to a **common denominator** before squaring and comparing.

notes.title: Exam tip
notes.text: Always find the **longest side** first — only that side could possibly be the hypotenuse.
